title: E. Sims Campbell and why black writers wrote little on jazz
summary: Question of black critics, Preston Jackson's articles, and George Gaynor's writing.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: How about E. Sims Campbell? Do you know anything about E. Sims Campbell? He wrote the chapter on blues. I've seen him once. I never did really know him.
He was around New York. He was a cartoonist, you know. I think he did sketches or things for Esquire for a while, and I hadn't heard anything about him for years either.

He was a black writer. Yeah. Yeah. Which leads to a question I have. All right. Well, what, are there any black critics or writers of jazz that you are particularly interested in? Or would you venture to say why you don't think more blacks have written about their own creations?
Well, I just don't know. I've never, actually, I've read so little the last few years that even people like, say, Leroy Jones and all those who went in,
for blues in particular. But I've read a little, but not very much of their work either, actually.

As a matter of fact, Leroy Jones wrote an article, wrote a chapter in his book, Blues People, talking about jazz. He called it Jazz and the White Critics. He wanted to point out the fact that jazz, as a black art, not exclusively, but in large part in some respects. It's always been brought to the attention by white critics.
One of the earliest guys that wrote on jazz in New Orleans, of course, was Preston Jackson. That's right.
I was thinking about that, too.

Used to write all these articles for the Hot Jazz, Panacea's Magazine, back in the early, not necessarily early 30s, the middle 30s in particular. By 1935 or so, he was maybe before. I don't know how long before.
Paul Barnes kept a journal way, way back. Paul Barnes, who I would like to talk to. It's a shame we lost that.

George Gaynor could have written stuff. He was a pretty good writer. He could write poetry, and the song lyrics maybe aren't too original, but in short stories. He did have even short stories published, I know.
I enjoyed that poem called My Music. Did you ever read that?

I have it copied out somewhere in one of my notebooks up at school. I kept all kind of odd things like that if they appealed to me when I had more energy. Now I let the tape recorder do it. Excuse me, go ahead.

One of the funniest things is a little thing he made on his 60th birthday about, I think it was, about jazz when they hear it up on the moon. Did you ever hear that thing? I have a tape of it. No. You just hear that. It's a pretty funny thing.
Maybe I have. Satellite Blues or something?
No, it's a whole half hour tape.
No, no. I've never heard that.
